summary: Describes four optional security service extensions for S/MIME, which add extra features beyond basic signing and encryption, such as receipts and labels.

eli5.summary: Extra stickers for secure email, like a delivery receipt showing the message was received, or a label telling how secret it is.

how do encrypted mailing lists avoid loops
subtitle: Four optional add-ons for S/MIME email: signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing lists and signing-certificate binding.

tldr.problem: Basic S/MIME can sign and encrypt mail, but it cannot prove a message was received, mark how sensitive it is, let mailing lists handle encrypted mail safely, or bind a signer's exact certificate into the signature.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new signed attributes and procedures for four services (signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing lists and signing certificates), built around the idea of a message that is signed, then encrypted, then signed again.
tldr.outcome: Mail clients and mail list agents gain a standard way to return verifiable receipts, enforce access rules from labels, expand encrypted lists without loops, and resist certificate substitution. RFC 5035 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 2634 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1999 and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 5035, so read the two together.

sections.title: Four Optional Services for S/MIME
sections.content:
RFC 2634 describes four optional extensions to S/MIME: signed receipts, security labels, secure mailing lists and signing certificates. They extend S/MIME version 3 (the message and certificate specifications RFC 2633 and RFC 2632), and some can also be added to S/MIME version 2.

The first three services give functionality similar to the Message Security Protocol (MSP4), but the RFC says they are useful in many other environments, particularly business and finance. Signing certificates are useful wherever certificates travel with signed messages.

Compatibility is one-directional. A version 3 recipient can still read messages from a version 2 sender, but some extensions make messages from a version 3 sender unreadable by a version 2 recipient. The document defines both procedures and the ASN.1 attributes needed.
sections.eli5: This RFC adds four optional extras to secure email, like add-on stickers for a sealed envelope. Older mail programs may not understand some of the stickers.

sections.title: Triple Wrapping
sections.content:
Several services rely on a triple wrapped message: signed, then encrypted, then signed again. The two signers may be the same entity or different ones, and S/MIME does not limit nesting, so there may be more than three wrappings.

Each layer has a job. The inside signature gives content integrity, non-repudiation with proof of origin, and binds attributes such as a security label to the original content. Receipt requests live here. The encrypted body gives confidentiality, including for the attributes in the inside signature. The outside signature authenticates information processed hop by hop, for example by mail list agents, and binds attributes to the encrypted body for access control and routing.

The RFC lists the eight steps to build one: start with the original content, add MIME headers, sign, add a MIME construct (the inside signature), encrypt, add MIME headers, sign again and add a MIME construct (the outside signature). Either multipart/signed or application/pkcs7-mime may be used for the signatures, so receiving agents MUST be able to interpret both.

Attributes also have placement rules. For example, receiptRequest and msgSigDigest are inner only, mlExpansionHistory is outer only, and a signerInfo MUST NOT include multiple instances of any attribute type defined here. Each of these attributes MUST carry exactly one value.
sections.eli5: Imagine writing a letter and signing it, putting it in a locked box, then signing the box too. The inner signature vouches for the letter. The outer one vouches for the box as it passes through helpers.

sections.title: Signed Receipts
sections.content:
A signed receipt gives the originator proof of delivery and lets them show a third party that the recipient could verify the original signature. Because the receipt is bound to the original message through its signature, receipts can be requested only for signed messages. The receipt sender may also encrypt it.

The originator adds a receiptRequest attribute to the signed attributes of the inner signature. It holds a signedContentIdentifier (a unique ID), a receiptsFrom choice (all recipients, first-tier recipients only, or a specific list) and receiptsTo (where receipts go). Receipts may be requested only for the innermost SignedData layer, and a receipt MUST NOT itself request a receipt.

A recipient MUST verify the signature covering the request before acting on it. If verified requests conflict, it MUST NOT return any receipt. To build the receipt, the recipient copies the content type, the content identifier and the original signature value into a Receipt structure, digests it, and signs it along with a msgSigDigest attribute. That attribute carries the digest of the original signed attributes, so the sender can confirm the recipient saw exactly what was sent. The Receipt version is 1.

The sender must keep either the original SignedData or the digest values needed to validate returned receipts. Each recipient SHOULD return only one receipt, but senders SHOULD accept several. The RFC also defines contentHints, which describes the inner content on the outer signature, and contentReference, which links one SignedData to another, such as a reply to its original.
sections.eli5: It works like a certified-mail slip. The receiver signs a note that quotes a secret fingerprint of your letter, so you can prove they really got the exact same letter.

sections.title: Security Labels
sections.content:
A security label describes how sensitive a message is, so a receiving agent can compare it with the user's authorizations and decide whether to show the content. Labels may also serve as routing information. They often describe ranked levels such as secret or confidential, or roles such as a patient's health-care team.

The eSSSecurityLabel attribute holds a required security-policy-identifier plus optional classification, privacy mark and categories. The label MUST be a signed attribute, never unsigned, and a signerInfo MUST NOT have more than one. If any signerInfo in a SignedData has a label, all of them MUST, with identical values. An inner label covers the plaintext content; an outer label covers the encrypted message for access control and routing.

The classification integers are only meaningful under the named policy. Values 0 to 5 are reserved for the X.411 basic hierarchy, and a policy SHOULD NOT use them for anything else. The privacy mark is not used for access control.

An equivalentLabels attribute lets a trusted signer translate a label into another organization's policy. Receivers MUST ignore it if they understand the original label, and MUST NOT act on it unless the signature validates and the signer is trusted to translate.
sections.eli5: A security label is a sticker on a folder saying who may open it, like 'staff only'. Different offices can agree that their stickers mean the same thing.

sections.title: Secure Mailing Lists
sections.content:
Sending encrypted mail to a big group is costly, because the sender must build recipient-specific data for each person. A Mail List Agent (MLA) appears to the sender as a normal recipient, then does the per-recipient work and redistributes the message to list members.

Loops are a danger: if list A is a member of list B and B a member of A, mail cascades endlessly. To prevent this, the MLA records itself in an mlExpansionHistory attribute on the outer signature. Each entry (MLData) holds the list's identifier, the expansion time and an optional receipt policy. If an MLA sees its own identifier in the history, it MUST stop expanding and should warn a human administrator. The history may hold at most 64 entries.

An MLA MUST parse all layers, fully process any security labels (including access checks) before distribution, and always sign the outgoing message in a new outer SignedData layer, carrying over the earlier outer attributes unless it replaces them. It never changes data covered by an inner signature.

A list can also override the originator's receipt request with an mlReceiptPolicy: none, insteadOf (send receipts to another list of recipients) or inAdditionTo (also send to more recipients). A list cannot create a receipt request the originator did not make.
sections.eli5: A mailing list agent is like a class monitor who makes copies of a note for every kid. It writes its name on the note so that if the note comes back around, it knows to stop copying.

sections.title: The Signing Certificate Attribute
sections.content:
In CMS, the certificate a signer wants used to verify a signature is not itself covered by that signature. The signingCertificate attribute fixes this by placing certificate identifiers among the signed attributes.

The RFC describes three attacks: substitution of one certificate for another (a denial of service, or a swap to a valid certificate with the same public key but different constraints), reissue of a certificate by a CA with different attributes, and a rogue duplicate CA. The attribute is designed to stop simple substitution and reissue of end-entity certificates, and to turn substitution into only a denial of service. It does not attempt to solve every attack; the real defense against a rogue CA is never to trust it.

The attribute contains a list of ESSCertID values, each with a SHA1 hash of the entire DER-encoded certificate and an optional issuer and serial number, plus optional policy information. The first entry MUST be the certificate used to verify the signature, and if its hash does not match, the signature MUST be considered invalid. Any later entries limit which authorization certificates (attribute certificates or other public key certificates) may be used. The attribute MUST be signed.
sections.eli5: It is like writing on a signed check which exact ID card you showed the bank. Nobody can swap in a different ID card later and claim it was the one used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations of CMS and S/MIME version 3 also apply. The RFC adds several warnings of its own.

  • Do not reply to receipt requests that cannot be validated, or that conflict, since an attacker may have inserted them. A reply to an unvalidated sender can expose information about the recipient.
  • Senders should consider encrypting receipts, to deny a passive attacker what they reveal.
  • Senders must not rely on recipients to honor security labels. Many S/MIME clients will not understand them and will still display a labelled message.
  • A receiving agent that hides a message because of its label must make sure the content cannot be seen later, for example inside a bounced error message.
  • A man-in-the-middle holding a signature the recipient can validate could add receipt destinations to a message and so receive receipts.
  • Encrypted mailing lists without the Section 4 mechanisms can be looped by subscribing one list to another, and MLAs can be abused as oracles for the adaptive chosen ciphertext attack described in CMS. They should notify an administrator if many undecryptable messages arrive.
  • Verify only with certificates already known to be valid or taken from a signed SigningCertificate attribute.
sections.eli5: Don't trust a sticker or a slip unless you checked who signed it. A sticker saying 'secret' won't stop a careless mail program from showing the letter, and a secret letter must not leak in a bounced-back copy.
